lines.text: June 2026. A three-week-old calf in Zavala County, Texas, is found with maggots in its navel.
Not ordinary maggots. These eat living flesh.
The New World screwworm. America wiped it out in 1966. Now it's back.
And the weapon that beat it last time wasn't a poison. It was more flies. Billions of them.
Here's how it works. A female lays two hundred fifty to five hundred eggs at the edge of a wound, or a newborn's navel.
The maggots burrow into healthy flesh. Disturb them, and they screw in deeper. That's the name.
The wound draws more flies. Left alone, it can kill the animal.
Cattle, deer, dogs, cats. Even, sometimes, people.
In good years, it spread all the way to the Canadian border.
In the nineteen thirties, two government scientists, Edward Knipling and Raymond Bushland, went looking for a better way to fight it.
And they found a weakness. A female screwworm mates only once in her life.
So what if her one mate was sterile? Flood the land with sterile males, and wild females lay eggs that never hatch.
But how do you sterilize a fly? The clue came from a book by Nobel laureate Hermann Muller, on radiation and genes.
Bushland borrowed an army X-ray machine in Kerrville, Texas. In six months, he had the dose.
They published in 1951.
A first test on Sanibel Island, Florida, backed the idea. But Sanibel sits right off the coast. They wanted proof.
So, in 1954, they went to Curaçao, an island in the Caribbean. Every week, an airplane dropped sterile flies over it.
After three weeks, about seventy percent of the egg masses they found were sterile. Within about two months, fertile eggs were gone.
In 1955, the results and the theory went to print, side by side.
Then they scaled up. Florida first, in 1958. Then the whole Southwest.
By 1966, the screwworm was gone from the United States. Over the next decade, America and Mexico released more than ninety four billion sterile flies.
Mexico was declared free in 1991. Then, country by country, Central America.
Today, a plant in Panama releases up to a hundred million sterile flies a week, a living wall at the Darién Gap.
Even when it slipped into the Florida Keys in 2016, attacking endangered Key deer, it was beaten by March 2017.
Then, in late 2024, the wall broke. Screwworms showed up in southern Mexico, and started moving north.
In July 2025, the US closed the border to Mexican cattle.
The fly kept coming. Seventy miles from the border. Then thirty one.
Then, June third, 2026. Texas.
By the end of October, seventy one cases. Texas, New Mexico, Arizona. Cattle, and dogs, and a cat.
So America is doing what worked before. Sterile flies are dropping over Texas again.
And a new fly factory at Moore Air Base in Edinburg, Texas, is meant to start by the end of this year. A hundred million flies at first. Three hundred million by 2028.
If you have animals, check their wounds. Report maggots to a vet or the USDA. And no, your beef is safe.
We beat this fly once, not with poison, but with one strange fact. She only mates once. Now, we have to do it again.
